1.source: Zhuangzi, ch. 13 (Tian dao, The Way of Heaven)
1.title: The Wheelwright's Hand
1.quote: 得之於手而應於心，口不能言，有數存焉於其間
1.quoteEn: The hand gets it and the heart answers. The mouth cannot say it. Yet there is a knack in there.
1.body: Wheelwright Bian tells a duke that the book in his hands is the dregs of dead men. His proof is his own trade. Cut the wheel too slowly and the fit is loose. Cut too fast and it jams and will not go in. The right speed lives in his hand, and he cannot give it even to his son. The Laozi opens with the same wall: 道可道，非常道. Zhuangzi turns the wall into a workshop. The Way that cannot be said is not far off or misty. It is as close as a skill. What do your hands know that you could not write down?

1.title: Words Run Out
1.quoteEn: Writing does not exhaust speech. Speech does not exhaust meaning.
1.body: The Great Treatise agrees with the first line of the Laozi, and then takes a different road. If words fall short, it says, the sages set up images to carry the whole meaning: the broken and unbroken lines of the hexagrams. The Laozi offers no such tool. It says 名可名，非常名 and leaves the reader at the gate. So two old books meet the same limit. One builds a system of pictures to get past it. The other keeps pointing at the limit itself. Notice that the Laozi also thinks in images: valley, water, gate, infant. Is an image a kind of word, or something else?

2.source: Cao Xueqin, Story of the Stone, ch. 1 and ch. 5 (gate of the Great-Void Illusion Land)
2.title: The Gate of Illusion
2.quote: 假作真時真亦假，無為有處有還無。
2.quoteEn: When false is taken for true, true is also false. Where nothing is made into something, something turns back to nothing.
2.body: This couplet hangs on the stone arch of 太虛幻境, the Great-Void Illusion Land. A dreamer reads it in chapter 1 and the boy Baoyu reads it again in chapter 5. Its second line plays with the same pair as this passage: 有 and 無, having and not-having. The Laozi says 有無相生, each gives birth to the other. Cao Xueqin makes the same turn sound like a warning. The Laozi is calm about the pair. The novel is sad about it, because its people love what is 有 and will lose it. Note one more trick. The characters 無為 sit inside the line, but here they do not mean wu wei. They mean 'nothing is taken as'. Does the echo of the phrase still ring?

2.source: Zhuangzi, ch. 2 (Qi wu lun, Making Things Equal)
2.title: Born and Dying Together
2.quote: 方生方死，方死方生，方可方不可
2.quoteEn: At the moment of birth, dying. At the moment of dying, birth. At the moment of yes, no.
2.body: The Laozi says the opposites lean on each other: long and short, high and low, before and after. Zhuangzi pushes harder. He takes the two heaviest pairs, life and death, right and wrong, and says they also arise together. Each 'that' comes out of a 'this'. Then he draws a conclusion the Laozi leaves quiet: the sage does not walk down either side, and 'lights things up by heaven' instead. The Laozi's sage also steps back, into 無為之事 and 不言之教. Zhuangzi shows what the step feels like from inside. It feels like no longer needing to win the argument.

4.source: Musashi, Book of Five Rings, Void scroll (空之巻)
4.title: The Void as the Way
4.quote: 空を道とし、道を空とみる所也。
4.quoteEn: Take the void as the Way, and see the Way as void.
4.body: Musashi's last scroll is one page long, and this is its last line. The Laozi says 道沖, the Dao is empty like a bowl, and use does not fill it. Musashi's 空 is a Buddhist word, but he gives it a soldier's test. The true void is not confusion. It comes when the clouds of doubt clear after long training. So the two texts agree that the center is empty, and they differ on the road. The Laozi's emptiness is there from the start, 'ancestor of the ten thousand things'. Musashi's emptiness is earned, morning after morning. Is emptiness something found or something made?

5.source: Zhuangzi, ch. 14 (Tian yun, The Turning of Heaven)
5.title: Straw Dogs, Before and After
5.quote: 夫芻狗之未陳也，盛以篋衍，巾以文繡
5.quoteEn: Before the straw dogs are set out, they lie in a basket, wrapped in embroidered cloth.
5.body: The Laozi names straw dogs, 芻狗, and does not explain them. Zhuangzi does. Before the rite, the straw dogs are kept in a box under fine cloth, and the priest fasts before he touches them. After the rite, people walk on their heads, and the grass-cutters burn them for cooking. Nobody hates them. Their hour is over. This makes 天地不仁 less cold than it sounds in English. Heaven and earth are not cruel. They do not cling. Zhuangzi then uses the image as a joke on Confucius, who drags old rites into a new age and sleeps under yesterday's straw dogs. What are you still wrapping in embroidered cloth?

5.source: Cao Xueqin, Story of the Stone, ch. 5 (last song of the dream suite, Birds Each Fly to the Wood)
5.title: The Clean White Ground
5.quote: 好一似食盡鳥投林，落了片白茫茫大地真乾淨。
5.quoteEn: It is just like birds that fly to the wood when the food is gone. What is left is a wide white ground, truly clean.
5.body: In a dream, the boy Baoyu hears a suite of songs that tell the end of his family before it happens. This is the close of the coda. The officials fall, the rich lose their gold, each debt is paid, and then the stage is bare. The picture is the Laozi's 天地不仁 seen from inside a great house. Heaven and earth treat the Jia family as straw dogs: honored for a season, then let go. The novel does not call this cruel. It says 乾淨, clean. The Laozi says the space between heaven and earth is like a bellows, empty and never used up. Can a bare ground be a comfort?

6.source: Yijing, hexagram 2 Kun (The Receptive), Tuan commentary
6.title: The Field That Bears
6.quote: 至哉坤元，萬物資生，乃順承天。
6.quoteEn: How complete is the source in Kun! The ten thousand things take their birth from it, and it follows and receives heaven.
6.body: The Laozi's 谷神, the valley spirit, is called 玄牝, the dark female, and her gate is the root of heaven and earth. The Yijing has its own great female: 坤, six broken lines, the earth. Both give birth without effort and are never used up. But look at the difference in rank. In the Yijing commentary, Kun 'follows and receives heaven'. She is second. In the Laozi, the dark female is first; heaven and earth come out of her gate. The Laozi takes the receiving side and puts it at the root of everything. That was a bold move in a world that ranked heaven over earth.

7.source: Sunzi, Art of War, ch. 7 (Jun zheng, Armies Contending)
7.title: Set Out Last, Arrive First
7.quote: 後人發，先人至，此知迂直之計者也。
7.quoteEn: Set out after the other and arrive before the other. This is to know the plan of the crooked and the straight.
7.body: The Laozi says the sage puts the self behind and so comes to the front: 後其身而身先. Sunzi has almost the same words about a march. Take the long road, bait the enemy off the short one, start late, arrive first. The grammar is alike and the heart is not. Sunzi's general goes behind as a plan, in order to be first. The Laozi's sage goes behind because there is no private end to push: 以其無私. Then the text adds a line that sounds like Sunzi after all: 'so the private end is fulfilled'. Is the Laozi teaching selflessness, or the deepest strategy? The passage does not let you settle.

8.source: Musashi, Book of Five Rings, Earth scroll (地之巻), outline of the Water scroll
8.title: Water Takes the Vessel's Shape
8.quote: 水は方圓の器にしたがひ、一てきとなり、さうかひとなる。
8.quoteEn: Water follows the square or round vessel. It becomes one drop, and it becomes the wide blue sea.
8.body: Musashi names his second scroll after water and says: make the heart into water. His reason is close to 上善若水. Water has no shape of its own, so no shape defeats it. But see what each writer does with this. The Laozi praises water because it goes to the low places that people hate, and so it does not contend: 不爭. Musashi praises water because it fits any enemy and any ground, and so it wins. One man reads water as humility. The other reads it as readiness. Both are true of water. Which one do you see first?

8.source: Sunzi, Art of War, ch. 6 (Xu shi, Empty and Full)
8.title: The Army Shaped Like Water
8.quote: 夫兵形象水，水之行，避高而趨下
8.quoteEn: The form of an army is like water. Water in its course avoids the high and hurries to the low.
8.body: This is the closest that Sunzi comes to the Laozi's own words. Water runs from the high place to the low. An army should run from the enemy's full place to the empty one. The chapter goes on, in the edition used here: 'an army has no fixed force and no constant form'. The Laozi's water also 'dwells in places the crowd dislikes'. For the Laozi the low place is good in itself, near to the Dao. For Sunzi the low place is the gap in a wall. The same image serves peace in one book and attack in the other. This is why the two books are so often read together, and why they should not be mixed up.

8.source: Yijing, hexagram 29 Kan (The Pit, water doubled), Tuan commentary
8.title: Water in the Pit
8.quote: 水流而不盈，行險而不失其信。
8.quoteEn: Water flows on and does not fill up. It goes through danger and stays true.
8.body: The Yijing sees water in a darker place than the Laozi does. Hexagram 29 is water over water, a pit inside a pit. It is the sign of danger. Yet the comment finds the same virtue that the Laozi finds. Water keeps moving and never fills to the brim, and it stays true in a bad place. The Laozi's list of water's goods includes 言善信, 'in speech, good at being true'. The Yijing uses the same word, 信, for water in the gorge. So the Laozi's gentle water has already been through the pit. The softness is not innocence.

9.source: Cao Xueqin, Story of the Stone, ch. 13 (Qin Keqing's ghost warns Wang Xifeng)
9.title: The Moon When Full
9.quoteEn: The moon when full will wane. Water when full will spill.
9.body: A young wife of the Jia house dies in the night, and her spirit comes to the family's sharpest manager with two old sayings. The house has been bright for a hundred years, she says. Buy farmland around the ancestral graves now, and put the family school there. Land kept for the sacrifices is not seized even when a house is condemned. This is the Laozi's 持而盈之，不如其已 put to work in a household budget. The ghost does not ask for retreat from the world. She asks for a plan that expects the turn. Xifeng admires the speech and does nothing. The novel is, in one way, the story of that advice not taken. What would you set aside if you believed the moon was full?

9.source: Yijing, hexagram 1 Qian (The Creative), top line and its Image comment
9.title: The Dragon Too High
9.quoteEn: The dragon that has gone too high has regret. What is full cannot last.
9.body: The first hexagram tells the life of a dragon in six lines. It hides, appears, leaps, flies; in the third line a person toils all day in its place. The sixth line is the surprise. The dragon climbs past its place and there is regret. The comment gives the reason in four characters, and the key word is 盈, full, the same word the Laozi uses here. The Laozi says: when the work is done, step back; this is heaven's way, 功遂身退，天之道. The Yijing gives no advice at the top line. It only shows what happens to those who stay. Read the two together and the Laozi sounds less like a moral and more like weather.

10.source: Zhuangzi, ch. 4 (Ren jian shi, In the World of Men)
10.title: The Fasting of the Heart
10.quote: 氣也者，虛而待物者也。唯道集虛。
10.quoteEn: The breath is what is empty and waits for things. Only the Dao gathers in emptiness.
10.body: The Laozi asks: 專氣致柔，能嬰兒乎? Can you gather the breath, reach softness, and be like an infant? Zhuangzi gives the question a method and a name, 心齋, the fasting of the heart. Do not listen with the ear. Do not listen with the mind. Listen with the 氣, the breath, because the breath does not grasp. It only waits. The Laozi's passage is a row of questions with no answers. Zhuangzi answers one of them, in the mouth of Confucius, of all people. Try it for one conversation today. Listen without preparing a reply.

10.source: Musashi, Book of Five Rings, Void scroll (空之巻)
10.title: Polishing the Mirror
10.quote: 心意二ツの心をミがき、観見二ツの眼をとぎ
10.quoteEn: Polish the two hearts, mind and will. Sharpen the two eyes, the seeing-into and the looking-at.
10.body: The Laozi asks whether one can wash the dark mirror and leave no flaw: 滌除玄覽，能無疵乎. Musashi uses the same picture of cleaning. Polish the heart, sharpen the eye, until there is 'not the least cloud'. Then, he says, the true void appears. The two texts share the verb and split on the effort. The Laozi's question seems to wash by letting go. Musashi washes by drill, 'morning after morning, hour after hour'. A reader who trains the body will know both. Some dirt comes off with rest. Some comes off only with work. Which kind is on your mirror today?

11.source: Zhuangzi, ch. 4 (Ren jian shi, In the World of Men)
11.title: The Use of the Useless
11.quote: 人皆知有用之用，而莫知无用之用也。
11.quoteEn: All people know the use of the useful. No one knows the use of the useless.
11.body: The Laozi finds use in what is not there: the hub's hole, the pot's hollow, the room's door and window. 無之以為用. Zhuangzi takes the thought out of the workshop and gives it to a tree. A carpenter walks past a huge shrine oak without a glance. Its wood is worthless, he says: a boat of it sinks, a coffin rots, a door oozes sap, a pillar draws worms. So it has lived to a great age. The cinnamon tree is cut because it can be eaten. The Laozi's emptiness serves the cart and the house. Zhuangzi's uselessness serves the tree itself. He has changed the question from 'what makes a thing work?' to 'what lets a life last?'

11.source: Musashi, Book of Five Rings, Void scroll (空之巻)
11.title: Knowing What Is Not There
11.quote: ある所をしりて、なき所をしる、是則、空なり。
11.quoteEn: Know the place where something is, and so know the place where nothing is. This is the void.
11.body: Musashi defines his deepest word by the same pair as the Laozi: what is there and what is not. The Laozi says 有之以為利，無之以為用. What is there gives the gain; what is not there gives the use. A swordsman lives by this. The blade is 有. The gap in the other man's guard, the beat between two moves, the distance, are all 無, and the fight is decided there. Musashi adds a condition. You know the empty place only through the full one. No one sees the gap who has not studied the guard. Where is the working emptiness in the thing you do every day?

12.source: Cao Xueqin, Story of the Stone, ch. 12 (the Precious Mirror of Wind and Moon)
12.title: The Back of the Mirror
12.quote: 千萬不可照正面，只照他的背面
12.quoteEn: On no account look into the front. Look only into its back.
12.body: A lame Daoist gives a sick young man a mirror with two faces. The man is ill from desire for a woman who has tricked him. The back shows a skull. The front shows the woman, who waves him in. He looks at the front again and again, and dies. The Laozi says 五色令人目盲: the five colors make the eye blind. It also says the sage is 'for the belly, not for the eye'. Cao Xueqin's mirror makes the teaching a test, and the patient fails it. The novel also reports that the family blames the mirror and tries to burn it. Who gets blamed when the back of things shows the truth?

13.source: Cao Xueqin, Story of the Stone, ch. 19 (Baoyu to his maid Xiren)
13.title: A Puff of Smoke
13.quote: 等我化成一股輕煙，風一吹便散了的時候
13.quoteEn: Wait for the time when I have turned into a puff of light smoke, and one breath of wind blows it away.
13.body: Baoyu is a boy when he says this. Stay with me, he tells the maids, until I am ash. No, not ash, he adds; ash still has form and trace and knowing. Smoke. The Laozi says 吾所以有大患者，為吾有身; 及吾無身，吾有何患. I have great trouble because I have a self. Without a self, what trouble? Baoyu has reached the same thought by a child's road, through love and fear of loss. But the Laozi's line ends in care: who values the world as one's own body can be trusted with it. Baoyu's line ends in vanishing. Is 'no self' a way to hold the world, or to leave it?

14.source: Musashi, Book of Five Rings, Water scroll (水之巻), on the gaze in strategy
14.title: Two Ways of Seeing
14.quote: 観の目強く、見の目弱く、遠き所をちかく見、近き所を遠く見る事
14.quoteEn: Make the eye that sees into things strong and the eye that looks at things weak. See the far as near, and the near as far.
14.body: Musashi splits sight in two. 見 is the eye that fixes on a thing. 観 is the wide eye that takes in the whole field. He wants the second one strong. Know the enemy's sword, he says, without looking at the enemy's sword. The Laozi begins this passage with 視之不見: looked at, it is not seen. What it describes cannot be caught by the fixing eye. It has no top light and no bottom dark; it is 'the shape of no shape'. Musashi offers a bodily way in. Keep the eyeballs still and see both sides at once. Try it on a walk. What appears when the eye stops grabbing?

14.source: Zhuangzi, ch. 22 (Zhi bei you, Knowledge Wandered North)
14.title: If You Heard It, That Is Not It
14.quote: 道不可聞，聞而非也；道不可見，見而非也
14.quoteEn: The Dao cannot be heard; what is heard is not it. The Dao cannot be seen; what is seen is not it.
14.body: The Laozi gives three names to what the senses miss: 夷 for the unseen, 希 for the unheard, 微 for the ungrasped. Then it says the three merge into one. Zhuangzi's speaker, a figure called No-Beginning, turns the same list into a rule of logic. Whatever you saw was a seen thing, so it was not the Dao. Whatever you can say is a said thing. He ends: the Dao does not fit a name. The Laozi is gentler here. It follows the nameless back to 'the old beginning' and calls that the thread of the Dao. One text closes a door. The other hands you a thread.

15.source: Zhuangzi, ch. 5 (De chong fu, The Sign of Virtue Complete)
15.title: The Still-Water Mirror
15.quote: 人莫鑑於流水，而鑑於止水。
15.quoteEn: No one uses running water as a mirror. People use still water.
15.body: The Laozi asks: 孰能濁以靜之徐清? Who can take what is muddy and, by stillness, slowly make it clear? Zhuangzi adds what the clear water is for. People come to it to see themselves. In his story the still one is a man who has lost a foot, and yet he has as many followers as Confucius. He teaches nothing. They come as people come to a pond. So stillness is not only a private cure. It becomes a service, without any plan to serve. Think of the calmest person you know. What do people do near them?

15.source: Sunzi, Art of War, ch. 6 (Xu shi, Empty and Full)
15.title: Subtle to the Point of No Form
15.quote: 微乎微乎！至于無形；神乎神乎！至于無聲
15.quoteEn: Subtle, subtle, to the point of having no form! Spirit-like, spirit-like, to the point of having no sound!
15.body: The Laozi describes the masters of old as 微妙玄通，深不可識: subtle, wondrous, dark, reaching through, too deep to know. Sunzi praises his general in nearly the same breath, and with the same first word, 微. But Sunzi tells us what the hiddenness is for. The enemy does not know where to defend or where to attack, 'so he can be the master of the enemy's fate'. The Laozi's masters are unreadable because they are careful, like someone crossing a winter stream. They are not hiding a plan. They have no fixed shape to show. Is there a difference between being unreadable and being empty?

16.title: The Heart of Heaven and Earth
16.quoteEn: In Return, does one not see the heart of heaven and earth?
16.body: Hexagram 24 has one firm line at the bottom, under five yielding lines. It is the winter solstice: the first light coming back. The Laozi uses the same word, 復, in this passage. The ten thousand things rise together, and 吾以觀復, 'I watch them return'. Each goes home to its root, and going home is called stillness. Wang Bi wrote a famous note on the Yijing line that joins the two books. He said the heart of heaven and earth shows when movement rests. So for him 'return' pointed down into quiet, not up into growth. Later readers disagreed and saw new life in that one line. Which do you see at the turn of the year?

16.source: Story of the Stone, ch. 120 (Cheng-Gao continuation)
16.title: Back to the Great Waste
16.quoteEn: Vast and dim, vast and dim: going home to that Great Waste.
16.body: At the end of the novel, Baoyu's father sees him one last time on a snowy riverbank, between a monk and a Daoist. The three walk off singing. The song names the place where the stone began, Qinggeng Peak, and the Great Waste. The whole book has been one long loop out and home. The Laozi says 夫物芸芸，各復歸其根: things in their crowds each go back to the root. And: 歸根曰靜. The novel shows the cost that the Laozi does not count. A father stands in the snow. Does going back to the root always leave someone on the bank?

17.source: Zhuangzi, ch. 7 (Ying di wang, Fit for Emperors and Kings)
17.title: As If It Did Not Come from Him
17.quote: 功蓋天下而似不自己，化貸萬物而民弗恃
17.quoteEn: His work covers the world, yet it seems not to come from him. His changing reaches all things, yet the people do not lean on him.
17.body: Zhuangzi puts this in the mouth of Lao Dan, the Laozi figure himself. It reads like a comment on this passage. The best ruler is one the people barely know is there, and when the work is done they say 我自然: 'we did it ourselves'. Zhuangzi adds a detail: such a king 'lets things find their own joy' and stands where no one can measure him. The Laozi lists the worse kinds too: the loved, the feared, the despised. Think of the best teacher or manager you have had. Did you notice them at the time?

18.source: Zhuangzi, ch. 6 (Da zong shi, The Great Ancestral Teacher)
18.title: Fish on Dry Land
18.quote: 相呴以濕，相濡以沫，不如相忘於江湖。
18.quoteEn: They breathe damp on each other and wet each other with spit. Better to forget each other in the rivers and lakes.
18.body: The Laozi makes a hard claim: 大道廢，有仁義. When the great Dao is dropped, then there is 'kindness and right'. Zhuangzi gives the claim a picture that is hard to forget. The spring dries up. Fish lie together on the mud and keep each other wet. It is real kindness, and it is a sign of disaster. In deep water they would not need it and would not think of each other. The picture is fair to both sides. It does not mock the fish. It asks where the water went. When you see great devotion in a family or a team, look for the dry spring.

18.source: Cao Xueqin, Story of the Stone, ch. 36 (Baoyu on dying for a name)
18.title: The Minister Who Dies for a Name
18.quoteEn: There must first be a muddled ruler before he can protest.
18.body: Baoyu attacks the two proud deaths of his culture: the civil official who dies protesting and the soldier who dies in battle. A loyal protest, he says, needs a bad ruler to exist. So the man who seeks that death is seeking a name, and leaves his lord in a worse place. This is the Laozi's 國家昏亂，有忠臣 turned into a young man's rant, even with the same word, 昏, muddled. The Laozi states it as a symptom: loyal ministers appear when the state is dark. Baoyu makes it a charge against the ministers. He goes too far, and his maid tells him so. Is a virtue that needs a disaster still a virtue?

19.title: When the Sages Are Cut Off
19.quoteEn: So cut off the sage and throw away knowledge, and the great robbers will stop.
19.body: This chapter of the Zhuangzi quotes the Laozi's 絕聖棄智 and gives it teeth. Locks and seals, it says, protect a box from small thieves. The great thief carries off the whole box, locks and all. So the one who steals a state also steals its laws and its wise sayings, and is called a lord. Wisdom is the robber's best tool. The Laozi's own lines are short and end in a positive picture: 見素抱樸, show the plain silk, hold the uncarved wood. The Zhuangzi chapter is angrier and more political. It is probably by a later hand in Zhuangzi's school. Read the two and ask: who gains from the rules you admire?

19.source: Cao Xueqin, Story of the Stone, ch. 21 (Baoyu continues the Zhuangzi)
19.title: Baoyu Continues the Zhuangzi
19.quote: 焚花散麝，而閨閣始人含其勸矣
19.quoteEn: Burn the Flower, scatter the Musk, and then the women's rooms will keep their good advice to themselves.
19.body: One night, sulking after a quarrel with his maids, Baoyu reads the 'Rifling Trunks' chapter, the same one that quotes this passage of the Laozi. He takes up the brush and adds his own lines. 'Flower' and 'Musk' are two maids, Xiren and Sheyue. Destroy Baochai's beauty, he writes, dull Daiyu's wit, and the trouble of love will end. It is a parody, and a sharp one. The Laozi's 絕聖棄智 always sounds grand until someone applies it to the people he loves. Before the chapter ends, Daiyu finds the page and mocks it in a verse of her own. Can you 'cut off' what you are attached to with a slogan?

20.source: Cao Xueqin, Story of the Stone, ch. 3 (the mock verses on Baoyu, to the tune West River Moon)
20.title: The Useless Boy
20.quote: 無故尋愁覓恨，有時似傻如狂。
20.quoteEn: For no cause he hunts for sorrow and seeks out regret. At times he seems a fool, at times like a madman.
20.body: When Baoyu first walks into the novel, the narrator stops and gives two verses that 'fit him exactly'. They call him dull, stubborn, no use to state or family, and tell rich boys not to copy him. The Laozi's speaker in this passage draws the same portrait of himself: 我愚人之心也哉, 'mine is the heart of a fool'. The crowd is bright and busy as if at a feast; 我獨頑似鄙, 'I alone am stubborn and rough'. The verses about Baoyu even use the same word, 頑. In both texts the insult is a mask for praise. But the Laozi's fool is fed by 'the mother'. What feeds Baoyu?

20.source: Cao Xueqin, Story of the Stone, ch. 1 (the stone left over when Nüwa mended the sky)
20.title: The One Stone Left Over
20.quoteEn: It alone was without talent and not fit to be chosen.
20.body: The goddess Nüwa smelts 36,501 great blocks to mend the broken sky. She uses 36,500. One block is left at the foot of a peak. The smelting has given it a spirit, so it knows it was passed over, and it weeps day and night. The whole novel grows from this one rejected block. The Laozi's speaker in this passage stands in the same place. 眾人皆有餘，而我獨若遺: the crowd all have more than enough, and I alone seem left behind. 眾人皆有以: the crowd all have a use. The feeling differs. The stone grieves and begs to enter the world of the useful. The Laozi's speaker stays outside and prizes 食母, being fed by the mother. Both begin with the word 獨, alone. Is being passed over a wound or a shelter?

21.source: Zhuangzi, ch. 2 (Qi wu lun, Making Things Equal)
21.title: Zhuang Zhou and the Butterfly
21.quote: 周與胡蝶，則必有分矣，此之謂物化。
21.quoteEn: Between Zhou and the butterfly there must be some division. This is called the changing of things.
21.body: Zhuang Zhou dreams he is a butterfly, happy and sure. He wakes and is plainly Zhou. Then he cannot tell which one is dreaming the other. The Laozi says the Dao as a thing is 惟恍惟惚, only dim and only blurred, and yet 其中有象, 'within it there is an image', and within it something real and true. The two passages share a mood more than a claim, and we should say so. Both refuse to make the world sharper than it is. Zhuangzi keeps a distinction ('there must be some division') and still will not rank the two sides. The Laozi keeps a center in the blur. Can you hold a thing as real without holding it as fixed?

22.source: Zhuangzi, ch. 20 (Shan mu, The Mountain Tree)
22.title: The Straight Tree Is Cut First
22.quoteEn: The straight tree is felled first. The sweet well is drained first.
22.body: The Laozi opens with an old saying: 曲則全, the bent stays whole. Zhuangzi gives the other half of the picture, what happens to the unbent. The straight trunk makes a good beam, so the axe finds it. The sweet well serves everyone, so it runs dry. In the story a visitor says this to Confucius, who has shown off his learning and is now surrounded by enemies. The Laozi's own lines move from the tree to conduct: 不自見故明, 'not showing oneself, and so shining'. Neither text tells you to be crooked. They tell you what display costs. Where are you the sweet well?

22.title: The Inchworm Bends
22.quote: 尺蠖之屈，以求信也。龍蛇之蟄，以存身也。
22.quoteEn: The inchworm draws itself in so that it can stretch out. Dragons and snakes lie hidden in winter so that they keep their bodies whole.
22.body: The Laozi says 枉則直: the crooked becomes straight. The Great Treatise comes very close to this, and its example is small and exact. An inchworm cannot move forward at all unless it first bends double. Bending is not a setback before the motion. It is half of the motion. The same passage speaks of sun and moon, cold and heat, each going so the other can come. The Laozi stacks six such pairs: bent and whole, crooked and straight, hollow and full, worn and new, few and gaining, many and confused. Watch for the drawing-in phase of something in your life. Are you calling it failure?

23.title: The Sun at Noon
23.quote: 日中則昃，月盈則食，天地盈虛，與時消息
23.quoteEn: The sun at noon begins to slant. The moon when full begins to be eaten away. Heaven and earth fill and empty, growing and fading with the seasons.
23.body: The Laozi says a whirlwind does not last the morning and a rainstorm does not last the day. Who makes them? Heaven and earth. 天地尚不能久: even heaven and earth cannot make a thing last. The Yijing comment on the hexagram of Abundance says the same and ends with the same turn toward us: 'how much less can people?' Both texts use the sky to take the shame out of decline. Yet the hexagram's own advice is 'be like the sun at noon': shine fully while it is noon. The Laozi's advice here is to talk less. One says use the peak. One says do not force it. Can both be right?

24.source: Musashi, Book of Five Rings, Water scroll (水之巻), on footwork
24.title: Walk as You Always Walk
24.quote: 足つかひハ、ことによりて、大小遅速ハ有とも、常にあゆぶがごとし。
24.quoteEn: In footwork, the step may be large or small, slow or quick, as the case requires, but it is always like ordinary walking.
24.body: The Laozi says 企者不立，跨者不行: one on tiptoe does not stand firm, one with a long stride does not go far. Musashi lists three kinds of foot he dislikes: the jumping foot, the floating foot, and the planted foot. Each is a way to add something to plain walking. In the Wind scroll he gives the reason. In a real fight the ground may be swamp, stones, or a narrow path, and tricks of the feet fail there. The Laozi calls such extras 'leftover food and useless growths' on the Dao. Both men trust the ordinary. Watch your own walk when you want to impress someone. What gets added?

25.source: Cao Xueqin, Story of the Stone, ch. 17 (Baoyu and his father in the new garden)
25.title: What 'Natural' Means
25.quote: 天之自然而有，非人力之所成也
25.quoteEn: It is what heaven has of itself. It is not something brought about by human effort.
25.body: Baoyu's father leads a party through the new garden and stops at a model farm village, with thatch, mud walls, and a well. He loves it. Baoyu asks the guests what the old word 天然 means. They give this definition, and it is a good one. It unpacks the last two characters of this passage: 道法自然, the Dao follows what is so of itself. Then Baoyu springs the trap. This farm was plainly forced into place by human hands, he says, with no village near it and no source for its stream. His father nearly throws him out. The Laozi's 自然 is easy to praise and hard to recognize. How much of what you call natural was arranged to look that way?

26.source: Musashi, Book of Five Rings, Water scroll (水之巻), on the state of the heart
26.title: Not Still When Still, Not Fast When Fast
26.quote: 静なるときも、こゝろハしづかならず、何と早き時も、心ハ少もはやからず。
26.quoteEn: Even when all is quiet, the heart is not quiet. However fast things move, the heart is not fast at all.
26.body: The Laozi says 重為輕根，靜為躁君: the heavy is the root of the light, the still is the ruler of the restless. A lord who travels all day does not leave his loaded wagons. Musashi describes the same ruler from inside a fight. The heart sits 'in the exact middle' and is not pulled along by the body. But he adds a point the Laozi does not make. The still heart is not a stopped heart. In quiet times it keeps moving, gently, like water that sways and does not stand. Stillness that rules is alive. Check yourself in the next rush: is your heart running at the speed of your hands?

27.source: Musashi, Book of Five Rings, Earth scroll (地之巻), the way of strategy compared to carpentry
27.title: The Master Carpenter Wastes Nothing
27.quote: 節有とも、ゆがミたりとも、強き木をば…能吟味してつかふ
27.quoteEn: Wood that is strong, even if it has knots, even if it is warped ... he looks at closely and puts to use.
27.body: Musashi compares a general to a master carpenter sorting timber. Straight, clean wood goes to the front pillars. Strong wood with knots goes to the back pillars. Weak but pretty wood becomes sills and sliding doors. Even bent and knotted wood finds its place if it is strong, and the worst becomes scaffolding and later firewood. The Laozi says of the sage: 常善救人，故無棄人; 常善救物，故無棄物. Always good at saving people, so no person is thrown away; always good at saving things, so no thing is thrown away. The Laozi calls this 'following the light'. Musashi calls it knowing your men. Who on your team have you filed as warped wood?

27.source: Zhuangzi, ch. 3 (Yang sheng zhu, The Lord of Nourishing Life)
27.title: Cook Ding Follows the Grain
27.quote: 官知止而神欲行，依乎天理
27.quoteEn: Knowing by the senses stops, and the spirit's own impulse moves, following the grain that heaven gave.
27.body: The Laozi says 善行無轍迹: a good walker leaves no track. A good knot needs no rope and cannot be untied. Cook Ding is the Zhuangzi's portrait of such skill. After years with the ox he no longer sees with the eye. He lets the knife go through the natural gaps, and it never meets bone. A common cook hacks and changes knives each month. Ding's knife is nineteen years old and as sharp as new. 'No track' here has a plain meaning: nothing was forced, so nothing was damaged, the ox or the blade. Look at the tracks your own work leaves. Where are you cutting across the grain?

28.source: Cao Xueqin, Story of the Stone, ch. 25 (the monk speaks to the jade)
28.title: The Stone Before It Was Clever
28.quote: 卻因鍛煉通靈後，便向人間覓是非。
28.quoteEn: But after the smelting made your spirit awake, you went among people to look for right and wrong.
28.body: A scabby monk holds Baoyu's jade and speaks to it as an old friend. Thirteen years ago, he says, you were a stone at the foot of a peak. Heaven did not bind you. You had no joy and no grief. Then you were refined and became clever, and you went looking for trouble. Now powder and rouge have dulled your light. The Laozi's word for the first state is 樸, the uncarved block, and its hope is 復歸於樸, to come back to it. It warns: 樸散則為器, when the block is split it becomes tools. The novel is that split told as one life. Is the return the same as never having left?

28.title: The Carpenter's Crime
28.quote: 夫殘樸以爲器，工匠之罪也
28.quoteEn: To wreck the uncarved wood in order to make vessels: this is the crime of the craftsman.
28.body: The Laozi says 樸散則為器 in a calm voice. The uncarved wood scatters and becomes tools, and the sage uses them to be chief of the officers. It ends with 大制不割: the great cutting does not sever. The 'Horses' Hooves' chapter takes the same two words, 樸 and 器, and makes them a charge. Carving the block is a crime. Breaking Dao and de to make 'kindness and right' is the sage's fault. The Laozi accepts that the block will be cut and asks for a cut that does not sever. The Zhuangzi chapter wants the block left alone. Which is closer to your view of schooling, or of management?

29.source: Cao Xueqin, Story of the Stone, ch. 5 (the song for Wang Xifeng, The Burden of Cleverness)
29.title: Schemes Run to the End
29.quote: 機關算盡太聰明，反算了卿卿性命。
29.quoteEn: Too clever, working every device to the end; the reckoning turned and took your own dear life.
29.body: Wang Xifeng runs the great Jia household. She is quick, funny, and afraid of nothing, and she fixes every problem by force of will and a hidden deal. Her song in the dream suite tells the result in two lines. The house falls 'like a great hall crashing'. The Laozi says of the world: 為者敗之，執者失之. Who works on it ruins it; who grips it loses it. It calls the world 神器, a spirit-vessel, a thing that cannot be handled. The novel shows this at the scale of one family. Xifeng is not punished by heaven. Her fixes are the cracks. What are you holding together by cleverness alone?

30.source: Sunzi, Art of War, ch. 3 (Mou gong, Attack by Stratagem)
30.title: Winning Without the Battle
30.quote: 不戰而屈人之兵，善之善者也。
30.quoteEn: To make the other side's army yield without a battle is the best of the best.
30.body: The Laozi says: one who helps a ruler with the Dao does not force the world with weapons. 果而勿強: get the result and do not press it. Sunzi, a general, writes that a hundred wins in a hundred battles is not the highest skill. On this the two books stand together against the love of glory. Yet they stand on different ground. Sunzi wants the enemy's state taken whole, because a whole prize is worth more. The Laozi looks at the land: 師之所處，荊棘生焉, where armies camp, thorns grow. One counts the cost to the winner. The other counts the cost to the field.

30.source: Musashi, Book of Five Rings, Wind scroll (風之巻), on other schools' 'strong sword'
30.title: The Sword Swung Hard
30.quote: 強きこゝろにて振太刀は、悪敷もの也。あらき斗にてハ勝がたし。
30.quoteEn: A sword swung with a 'strong' heart is a bad thing. With roughness alone it is hard to win.
30.body: Musashi mocks schools that teach a strong stroke. Try to cut hard and you cannot cut. Strike the other blade hard and your own blade breaks. Bring a strong army and the enemy brings one too. In his words, you do not win at anything without the principle of the Way. The Laozi's line is 果而勿強, and it closes with a law of bodies: 物壯則老, a thing at full strength grows old. Musashi killed men and the Laozi's author perhaps did not, yet they agree on force. Force is what you add when you have lost the line. Where do you push hardest? Is that where you are least sure?

31.source: Sunzi, Art of War, ch. 12 (Huo gong, Attack by Fire)
31.title: The Dead Do Not Come Back
31.quote: 亡國不可以復存，死者不可以復生。
31.quoteEn: A state that has perished cannot be made to exist again. The dead cannot be brought back to life.
31.body: Readers who think of Sunzi as cold should read the end of his chapter on fire. Anger can turn back into joy, he says. A lost state and a dead man cannot turn back. So the wise ruler is careful. The Laozi goes one step past him. 兵者不祥之器: weapons are tools of ill omen. Even a win is to be marked with the rites of a funeral, 戰勝以喪禮處之, and the killing of many is to be wept over. Sunzi gives a reason not to start. The Laozi gives a way to stand afterward. Is there a win in your past that you have never mourned?

31.source: Musashi, Book of Five Rings, Earth scroll (地之巻)
31.title: The Root Is to Surpass
31.quote: 武士の兵法をおこなふ道ハ、何事におゐても、人にすぐるゝ所を本とし
31.quoteEn: The warrior's way of practicing strategy takes as its root, in every matter, being better than others.
31.body: Here Musashi and the Laozi part, and it is good to see it clearly. For Musashi, winning is the point: in a duel, in a battle, for one's lord and for one's own name. Strategy that does not help when it counts is not the true way. The Laozi says 勝而不美: win, and do not find it beautiful. One who delights in killing cannot have his will in the world. Musashi is honest about the trade he is in. The Laozi is honest about what that trade does. A reader does not have to choose in the abstract. Ask it of one thing you compete at. What is the winning for?

32.source: Cao Xueqin, Story of the Stone, ch. 1 (the monk turns the stone into a jade)
32.title: A Few Words Carved
32.quote: 還只沒有實在的好處，須得再鐫上數字
32.quoteEn: Only it still has no real merit. A few characters must be carved on it too.
32.body: The stone begs to see the human world. A monk shrinks it into a bright jade that fits in the hand. Then he says this. A fine form is not enough; it needs writing on it, so that people 'will know at a glance that it is a rare thing'. The joke is quiet and deep. Value in the human world needs a label. The Laozi says 道常無名，樸: the Dao is always nameless, an uncarved block. And then 始制有名: when the cutting begins, there are names. Once there are names, it adds, know when to stop. The jade's whole trouble starts with its inscription. What was carved on you, and by whom?

33.source: Sunzi, Art of War, ch. 3 (Mou gong, Attack by Stratagem)
33.title: Know the Other, Know Yourself
33.quoteEn: Know the other and know yourself, and in a hundred battles there is no danger.
33.body: The Laozi weighs two kinds of knowing: 知人者智，自知者明. To know others is cleverness. To know oneself is light. Sunzi puts the same two side by side and asks for both, in that order, other first. He is counting forces before a fight. The Laozi ranks them. Self-knowledge gets the better word, 明, the word for sun and moon together. Then it does the same with winning: 自勝者強, the one who overcomes the self is the strong one. Sunzi's sentence makes you safe in a hundred battles. The Laozi's makes you need fewer. Which do you study more, your rivals or yourself?

33.source: Musashi, Book of Five Rings, Water scroll (水之巻), closing words
33.title: Beat Yesterday's Self
33.quote: 今日ハ昨日の我に勝、あすハ下手に勝、後ハ上手に勝と思ひ
33.quoteEn: Think: today I beat the self of yesterday; tomorrow I beat one less skilled; later I beat one more skilled.
33.body: The Laozi says 勝人者有力，自勝者強: who overcomes others has force; who overcomes the self is strong. Musashi, who by his own count fought over sixty duels, puts the self first in his order of training. The first opponent each day is yesterday's you. Only after that come the weaker and then the better fighters. He says this near the famous line about a thousand days of practice to forge and ten thousand to temper. The Laozi names the inner win as the real one and stops there. Musashi makes it step one of a ladder that still leads to beating others. Does the inner win stay inner if it is training for the outer one?

34.source: Zhuangzi, ch. 22 (Zhi bei you, Knowledge Wandered North)
34.title: Lower Still
34.quoteEn: 'How can it be still worse?' He said: 'It is in the shit and piss.'
34.body: Master Dongguo asks Zhuangzi where the Dao is. Everywhere, says Zhuangzi. Be specific. In the ant. So low? In the weeds. Lower? In the roof tile. Then this, and Dongguo stops answering. The Laozi says 大道氾兮，其可左右: the great Dao floods; it can go left or right. It clothes and feeds the ten thousand things and does not act as their lord, so it may be named among the small. Zhuangzi tests whether we mean it. 'Everywhere' is easy to say with mountains in mind. He walks the word downhill until it offends. Where is the place you would not expect to find it?

35.source: Zhuangzi, ch. 20 (Shan mu, The Mountain Tree)
35.title: Friendship Plain as Water
35.quote: 君子之交淡若水，小人之交甘若醴
35.quoteEn: The friendship of the noble is plain like water. The friendship of the small is sweet like new wine.
35.body: The Laozi says music and good food make the passing traveler stop. But the Dao, when it comes out of the mouth, is 淡乎其無味: plain, without taste. Look and there is not enough to see. Use it and it does not run out. Zhuangzi applies the same word, 淡, to friendship. The plain kind draws people close. The sweet kind ends in a break, because what joined for no deep reason parts for no deep reason. The saying is now a common proverb in Chinese. Both texts ask us to trust what does not advertise. Which of your friendships tastes of nothing and has lasted the longest?

36.source: Sunzi, Art of War, ch. 1 (Ji, Reckoning)
36.title: Able, Show Unable
36.quote: 能而示之不能，用而示之不用
36.quoteEn: When able, show them you are unable. When using your force, show them you are not using it.
36.body: This passage of the Laozi sounds the most like a war manual. 將欲歙之，必固張之: what you want to shrink, you must first stretch. What you want to weaken, first strengthen. Sunzi's first chapter has the same method stated as a craft: 'war is the way of deceit'. Some later readers, the Legalist Han Fei among them, took the Laozi here as a book of statecraft tricks. Others read the lines as a description of how things turn by themselves, with the lesson 柔弱勝剛強: the soft and weak overcome the hard and strong. The text ends by saying the state's sharp tools must not be shown. Is that a rule for the trickster, or a warning against owning such tools?

36.title: The Sage as Sharp Tool
36.quote: 彼聖人者，天下之利器也，非所以明天下也。
36.quoteEn: Those sages are the sharp tools of the world. They are not something to hold up to the world's light.
36.body: The 'Rifling Trunks' chapter quotes the end of this passage word for word: fish must not leave the deep, and 國之利器不可以示人, the state's sharp tools must not be shown to people. Then it gives its own answer to an old puzzle: what are the sharp tools? Not weapons, it says. The sages themselves, and their clever methods. Once wisdom is on display, robbers take it up along with everything else. This is one of the earliest readings of the Laozi line that we have. It shows the passage was already being argued over within a few generations. What skill of yours becomes dangerous when it is put on show?

38.source: Zhuangzi, ch. 22 (Zhi bei you, Knowledge Wandered North)
38.title: Down the Ladder
38.quote: 仁可爲也，義可虧也，禮相僞也
38.quoteEn: Kindness can be put on. Right conduct can be chipped away. In rites, people deceive each other.
38.body: This Zhuangzi chapter quotes the passage almost whole: lose the Dao and then comes de, then kindness, then right, then rites, and rites are 'the flower of the Dao and the head of disorder'. The speaker here is the Yellow Emperor, and he adds a short reason for each step down. The verbs get worse as he goes: put on, damaged, faked. The Laozi's own verdict on rites is 忠信之薄: they are the thin edge of loyalty and trust. Notice what neither text says. Neither says kindness is bad. Each says that when kindness needs a name and a rule, something earlier has already gone. What rule in your house stands in for a trust that is missing?

38.source: Musashi, Book of Five Rings, Earth scroll (地之巻)
38.title: More Flower Than Fruit
38.quote: 花實の二つにして、花よりもミのすくなき處なり。
38.quoteEn: Of the two, flower and fruit, there is less fruit than flower.
38.body: Musashi looks at the martial schools of his day and sees shops. They decorate the art, 'make it bloom', show off technique, and open one training hall after another for profit. The Laozi ends this passage with the same pair of words. The great person 處其實，不居其華: stays in the fruit and does not live in the flower. In the Laozi, 華 is its name for foreknowledge, the showy end of a long decline. In Musashi it is a fancy stroke that will not cut. Each took the image from the orchard, where a tree in heavy bloom tells you nothing about the harvest. In your own work, which part is flower?

39.title: Clear by Not Doing
39.quote: 天无爲以之清，地无爲以之寧
39.quoteEn: Heaven does nothing, and by this it is clear. Earth does nothing, and by this it is at rest.
39.body: Set this beside the Laozi's lines: 天得一以清，地得一以寧. Heaven got the One and by it is clear; earth got the One and by it is at rest. The frame of the sentence is the same, and one term has been changed. Where the Laozi has 'got the One', the Zhuangzi has 无爲, wu wei. The later text seems to be reading the earlier one and telling us what 'the One' is in practice. It is not a thing that heaven holds. It is heaven's way of not meddling. The Zhuangzi goes on: the two not-doings join, and all things are transformed. Which reading helps you more: a One to hold, or a doing to drop?

40.title: No Plain Without a Slope
40.quoteEn: There is no level ground without a slope. There is no going without a return.
40.body: The Laozi puts its whole physics in five characters: 反者道之動, turning back is the motion of the Dao. The Yijing puts the same law in the middle of its happiest hexagram. Peace is earth above heaven, the two in full exchange. At the third line, the point of greatest ease, the text says this. It does not say peace will fail. It says the slope is part of the plain. Then it adds what the Laozi leaves out: stay firm in hardship, do not lose faith, and there will be blessing in your daily bread. The Laozi's second line is 弱者道之用: weakness is how the Dao works. Does knowing the return spoil the plain, or let you enjoy it?

41.source: Musashi, Book of Five Rings, Water scroll (水之巻), the teaching of stance and no-stance
41.title: A Stance That Is No Stance
41.quote: 搆ハ有て搆ハなき、と云利也。
41.quoteEn: This is the principle called: there is a stance, and there is no stance.
41.body: Musashi teaches five sword positions and then says not to believe in them. Raise the middle guard a little and it is the high guard. Lower the high one and it is the middle. Hold the sword wherever it is easy to cut this enemy, on this ground. The form is real and it is not fixed. The Laozi's list of paradoxes ends in the same place: 大方無隅, the great square has no corners; 大象無形, the great image has no shape. A beginner needs the five positions. A master has them and is not in any of them. What form did you once need that you now hold loosely?

42.source: Cao Xueqin, Story of the Stone, ch. 31 (Shi Xiangyun teaches her maid)
42.title: Yin and Yang Are One Word
42.quote: 陽盡了就成陰，陰盡了就成陽
42.quoteEn: When yang is used up it becomes yin. When yin is used up it becomes yang.
42.body: Xiangyun and her maid Cuilü walk in the garden, and the maid asks why some flowers grow so strangely. Xiangyun answers with a lecture on yin and yang, and the maid's questions get funnier: does a brick have a yin side? Is a master yang and a maid yin? In the middle of the comedy comes real philosophy. There are not two things, says Xiangyun. The two words are one. It is not that yin ends and a separate yang is born. The Laozi says 萬物負陰而抱陽，沖氣以為和: all things carry yin on the back and hold yang in the arms, and the blended breath makes harmony. A girl in a garden, teasing her maid, has explained 'carry and hold'.

42.title: One Yin, One Yang
42.quoteEn: One yin, one yang: this is called the Dao.
42.body: This is the only passage in the Laozi that names yin and yang, and the Great Treatise has the most famous line about them. The two texts build the world in different orders. The Laozi counts down from above: 道生一，一生二，二生三，三生萬物. Dao gives birth to one, one to two, two to three, three to the ten thousand things. The Dao comes before the pair. The Treatise does not look behind the pair. The beat itself, now yin, now yang, is what it calls the Dao. So one book has a silent source, and the other has a rhythm with no source behind it. Do you sense something before the rhythm, or only the rhythm?

43.source: Zhuangzi, ch. 3 (Yang sheng zhu, The Lord of Nourishing Life)
43.title: What Has No Thickness
43.quote: 彼節者有間，而刀刃者无厚，以无厚入有間
43.quoteEn: Those joints have gaps, and the knife's edge has no thickness. What has no thickness enters where there is a gap.
43.body: The Laozi says 無有入無間: what has no being enters where there is no gap. Cook Ding says nearly the same thing about his knife, and makes it something you can watch. An ox looks solid. To a trained hand it is full of spaces. An edge thin enough finds 'plenty of room to play'. The Laozi goes further than the cook: it enters even where there is no gap at all, as water enters stone. From this it knows the gain of wu wei and of teaching without words. Ding's skill is the same lesson at a butcher's block. What hard problem in front of you has joints you have not looked for?

44.source: Cao Xueqin, Story of the Stone, ch. 1 (the lame Daoist's song, Hao liao ge)
44.title: Only Fame They Can't Forget
44.quote: 世人都曉神仙好，惟有功名忘不了
44.quoteEn: All people know it is good to be an immortal. Only fame and rank they cannot forget.
44.body: A lame, wild-haired Daoist walks down a street singing four verses. Each begins the same way and names one thing people cannot drop: rank, gold, a lovely wife, children. Each ends with what becomes of it. The great ministers are now a grave-mound under grass. The Laozi asks the same in three short questions: 名與身孰親? 身與貨孰多? Fame or your body, which is closer? Your body or goods, which is worth more? Its answer is 知足不辱，知止不殆: know what is enough and there is no shame; know when to stop and there is no danger. The song gives no answer. It just rhymes 好 with 了, good with over. Which verse is yours?

44.title: Tail in the Mud
44.quote: 寧其生而曳尾於塗中乎？
44.quoteEn: Or would it rather be alive and drag its tail in the mud?
44.body: Two officers find Zhuangzi fishing and offer him the government of Chu. He does not turn around. He asks about the sacred tortoise of Chu, dead three thousand years, kept wrapped in a box in the temple. Would that tortoise rather be honored bones, or alive in the mud? Alive, they say. Go away, says Zhuangzi. I will drag my tail in the mud. It is the Laozi's question 名與身孰親 acted out with a fishing rod in the hand. The Laozi argues it: great love costs much, great hoarding loses much. Zhuangzi makes the officers say the answer themselves. What honored box is being offered to you?

45.source: Musashi, Book of Five Rings, Wind scroll (風之巻), on other schools' use of speed
45.title: The Master Looks Slow
45.quote: 上手のする事ハ、緩々とミヘて、間のぬけざるところ也。
45.quoteEn: What a master does looks unhurried, and yet no beat is missed.
45.body: Musashi says speed is not part of the true way. A thing looks fast or slow only when it is off the rhythm. A courier who covers great distances does not run all day. A poor drummer feels a slow piece as rushed. A skilled hand never looks busy. The Laozi says 大巧若拙: great skill seems clumsy. And 大成若缺: great completion seems to lack something. Musashi explains the look from inside the craft. The master's work seems plain because nothing in it is extra, so there is nothing to admire but the result. The passage also says 清靜為天下正. Whose work have you thought slow that was in truth exact?

46.source: Cao Xueqin, Story of the Stone, ch. 2 (couplet at the ruined Zhitong temple)
46.title: Too Late to Draw Back the Hand
46.quote: 身後有餘忘縮手，眼前無路想回頭。
46.quoteEn: With plenty stored behind you, you forget to draw back your hand. With no road left before your eyes, you think of turning round.
46.body: A clever official who lost his post some time ago walks past a broken temple and reads this on its gate. He thinks: plain words, deep meaning; someone inside must have 'turned a somersault' in life. He goes in and finds only a deaf old monk cooking gruel, and loses interest. The Laozi says 禍莫大於不知足: no disaster is greater than not knowing what is enough. And 知足之足，常足矣: the enough of knowing-enough is always enough. The couplet says when people learn this. Too late. The scene adds a second lesson. The man reads the warning, praises it, and walks on, back into the world of office. How many true sentences have you admired and passed?

46.source: Zhuangzi, ch. 1 (Xiao yao you, Free and Easy Wandering)
46.title: One Branch, One Bellyful
46.quote: 鷦鷯巢於深林，不過一枝；偃鼠飲河，不過滿腹。
46.quoteEn: The wren nests in the deep forest and uses no more than one branch. The mole drinks at the river and takes no more than a bellyful.
46.body: The sage-king Yao offers the whole world to the hermit Xu You, and this is the refusal. A forest is of no use to a bird beyond its one branch. A river is of no use to a mole beyond a full belly. The Laozi states the same thing as a law: 知足之足，常足矣. In this passage it also shows the two worlds. With the Dao, fine horses are sent back to manure the fields. Without it, war-horses breed at the border. Zhuangzi makes 'enough' a matter of the body's true size. The wren is not being modest. A second branch is simply no good to it. What is your one branch?

47.source: Musashi, Book of Five Rings, Earth scroll (地之巻)
47.title: From One, Know Ten Thousand
47.quote: 一を以て万を知る事、兵法の利也。
47.quoteEn: To know ten thousand things by means of one: this is the principle of strategy.
47.body: The Laozi says 不出戶，知天下: without going out the door, know the world. Without looking through the window, see heaven's way. The farther one goes, the less one knows. Musashi makes a like claim for the sword. Learn truly how to defeat one man and you know how to defeat a thousand, as a builder raises a great Buddha from a one-foot model. He also says that he took the principle of strategy into all arts and skills, and in none of them had a teacher. Both men trust depth over range. But Musashi's 'one' is a practice done for decades with the whole body. Is the Laozi's sage also practicing something behind that closed door?

47.source: Sunzi, Art of War, ch. 13 (Yong jian, The Use of Spies)
47.title: Knowledge Must Come from People
47.quote: 不可取於鬼神…必取於人，知敵之情者也。
47.quoteEn: It cannot be had from ghosts and spirits ... it must be had from people, those who know the enemy's true state.
47.body: Here Sunzi flatly contradicts this passage, and the clash is useful. The Laozi says 其出彌遠，其知彌少: the farther you go out, the less you know. The sage knows without traveling. Sunzi says foreknowledge is what lets a wise ruler win, and it cannot be drawn from spirits, from likeness to past events, or from calculation. It comes from men sent out to look. Spies. The two are speaking of different knowing. Sunzi wants facts about a rival, which change each day. The Laozi wants the way things go, which does not. A mistake in life is to seek the first kind by sitting still, or the second kind by collecting reports. Which kind do you need today?

48.source: Zhuangzi, ch. 6 (Da zong shi, The Great Ancestral Teacher)
48.title: Sitting and Forgetting
48.quote: 墮枝體，黜聰明，離形去知，同於大通，此謂坐忘。
48.quoteEn: Let the limbs and body drop, dismiss hearing and sight, part from form, leave knowing behind, and be one with the great passage. This is called sitting and forgetting.
48.body: The Laozi says 為學日益，為道日損: in learning, each day a gain; in the Dao, each day a loss. Zhuangzi tells it as a report card. Yan Hui comes to Confucius three times. 'I am making progress. I have forgotten kindness and right.' Good, but not enough. 'I have forgotten rites and music.' Not enough. Then: 'I sit and forget.' Confucius is startled and asks to become Hui's student. The joke is that progress is measured in losses, and the best pupil of the school of learning is the one who shows it. The Laozi's line continues 損之又損, 'lose and again lose', until wu wei. What could you forget today and be better for it?

48.source: Musashi, Book of Five Rings, Water scroll (水之巻), closing words
48.title: A Thousand Days to Forge
48.quote: 千日の稽古を鍛とし、万日の稽古を錬とす。
48.quoteEn: Take a thousand days of practice as the forging, and ten thousand days of practice as the tempering.
48.body: Set this against 為道日損, 'in the Dao, each day a loss'. Musashi seems to stand on the other side: each day a gain, for thirty years. Yet look at what his training removes. He cuts away the fancy stances, the many techniques, the strong stroke, the fast stroke, the secret teachings. In the Wind scroll he says his school has no inner gate and no outer gate. And in his last page he says the void appears when the clouds of confusion clear. So the ten thousand days may be days of loss after all. A blade is tempered by burning out what is not steel. Is your practice adding to you, or uncovering you?

48.source: Cao Xueqin, Story of the Stone, ch. 1 (the lame Daoist explains his song)
48.title: Good Means Over
48.quote: 若不了，便不好，若要好，須是了。
48.quoteEn: If it is not over, it is not good. If you want it good, it has to be over.
48.body: Zhen Shiyin has lost his daughter and his house. He hears the Daoist's song and catches only two words, 好 and 了: 'good' and 'over'. The Daoist laughs. If you heard those two, you understood. Then he says this. 了 means finished, and it also means to see through a thing. The Laozi's road in this passage is 損之又損，以至於無為: lose and lose again, until you arrive at not-forcing. Both say that the good thing is on the far side of letting go. But the Daoist speaks to a man who has had it all taken from him. The Laozi speaks of a daily, chosen loss. Does loss teach the same thing when it is not chosen?

49.source: Zhuangzi, ch. 7 (Ying di wang, Fit for Emperors and Kings)
49.title: The Heart Used Like a Mirror
49.quote: 至人之用心若鏡，不將不迎，應而不藏
49.quoteEn: The perfected person uses the heart like a mirror. It does not see things off and does not go out to meet them. It answers and does not store.
49.body: The Laozi says 聖人無常心，以百姓心為心: the sage has no fixed heart, and takes the people's heart as the heart. To the good, the sage is good. To the not-good, the sage is also good. How can a person live so and not be worn out? Zhuangzi answers with the mirror. It gives each face back fully and keeps none. It does not lean toward what is coming or follow what has gone. 'So it can bear all things and is not hurt.' The Laozi's sage adds a warmth that a mirror lacks: the sage treats all people as children. Try the mirror in one hard meeting. Answer fully. Store nothing.

50.source: Musashi, Book of Five Rings, Earth scroll (地之巻)
50.title: Not Only the Warrior Dies Well
50.quote: 武士ハ只、死と云道を嗜事、と覚ほどの儀なり。
50.quoteEn: People seem to think that the warrior is simply one devoted to the way called dying.
50.body: Musashi reports the common view and then corrects it. Readiness to die, he says, is not special to warriors. Monks, women, and farmers also know duty and shame and can accept death. What marks the warrior is skill that prevails. The Laozi here speaks of one who is 善攝生, good at holding life. The rhinoceros finds no place for its horn in such a person, the tiger no place for its claws, the blade no place for its edge. Why? 以其無死地: there is no death-ground in that person. Both texts refuse to make death the hero. One answers with mastery. The other answers with something stranger, a life that offers no target. What would it mean to have no death-ground?

50.source: Cao Xueqin, Story of the Stone, ch. 63 (the nun Miaoyu's favorite lines, quoted from an older poet)
50.title: The Iron Threshold
50.quote: 縱有千年鐵門檻，終須一個土饅頭。
50.quoteEn: Though you have an iron threshold to last a thousand years, in the end you need one earth dumpling.
50.body: The 'earth dumpling' is a grave mound. Miaoyu, a proud young nun in the Jia garden, says that all poetry since the Han is worthless except these two lines. They come from the Song poet Fan Chengda, and the novel does not name him. So she signs her notes 'the one outside the threshold'. The Laozi asks why so many people walk into death. Its answer is 以其生生之厚: because they live life too thickly. An iron threshold is life made thick: gates, name, a house meant for a thousand years. Miaoyu sees through it. But she is also vain about seeing through it. Can one cling to non-clinging?

52.source: Zhuangzi, ch. 7 (Ying di wang, Fit for Emperors and Kings)
52.title: Seven Holes for Hundun
52.quote: 日鑿一竅，七日而渾沌死。
52.quoteEn: Each day they bored one opening. On the seventh day Hundun died.
52.body: Hundun, whose name means the unformed whole, is king of the center. The kings of the north and south seas visit him, and he treats them well. They want to repay him. All people have seven openings for seeing, hearing, eating, and breathing, they say; he alone has none. So they drill. The Laozi gives the same teaching as an instruction: 塞其兌，閉其門，終身不勤. Block the openings, shut the gates, and to the end of life you are not worn out. Open them and add to your affairs, and to the end there is no rescue. Zhuangzi's story shows the worst part. The drilling was a gift. Who is kindly boring holes in you, and in whom are you boring?

53.source: Musashi, Book of Five Rings, Wind scroll (風之巻), on other schools' 'inner' and 'outer' teachings
53.title: Nothing Hidden
53.quote: 此戦の道におゐて、何をかかくし、いづれをか顕さむ。
53.quoteEn: In this way of battle, what should one hide, and what should one reveal?
53.body: Other schools sold secret techniques and made students sign oaths. Musashi says there is no 'inner' in a real fight. You do not open with the surface moves and finish with the secret ones. If you go deep into a mountain and keep going, he says, you come out at the entrance again. The Laozi says 大道甚夷，而民好徑: the great road is very level, and people love the side paths. In this passage the side paths lead to a court with fine clothes, sharp swords, and empty granaries. Hidden teachings are side paths too. They please because they are hard to reach. What plain thing do you already know and avoid, because it is not a secret?

55.title: The Baby Grips All Day
55.quote: 終日握而手不掜，共其德也
55.quoteEn: It grips all day and the hand does not cramp. Its de is all of one piece.
55.body: The Laozi says of the infant: 終日號而不嗄，和之至也. It cries all day and is not hoarse; this is harmony at its peak. The Zhuangzi gives almost the same sentence to Lao Dan himself, at the end of a list of questions. The last question is 'Can you be a baby?' The Laozi also says of the infant 骨弱筋柔而握固: soft bones, supple sinews, and a firm grip. The Zhuangzi has that sign too, and adds one more. The baby grips all day and the hand does not cramp. It stares all day and the eye does not blink, because it is not caught by anything outside. The point is physical. Effort that comes from the whole body does not tire it. Watch a small child for five minutes. Where is the strain?

55.source: Story of the Stone, ch. 118 (Cheng-Gao continuation)
55.title: What Good Is an Infant?
55.quote: 那赤子有什麼好處，不過是無知無識無貪無忌。
55.quoteEn: What is so good about that newborn? Only that it has no knowing, no learning, no greed, and no dread.
55.body: Near the end, Baoyu sits reading the Zhuangzi, and his wife Baochai tries to argue him back to duty. He quotes Mencius on 'not losing the newborn's heart' and reads it this way. We are sunk in greed and love like mud, he says. Who can get back to the first step? Baochai answers that the sages meant a heart that cannot bear others' pain, not a heart that walks out on its family. The Laozi's line is 含德之厚，比於赤子: one who holds de in fullness is like a newborn. The couple are arguing over which infant is meant, the Confucian one or the Daoist one. Baoyu means the Laozi's. Soon after, he leaves. Was Baochai wrong?

56.title: Get the Meaning, Forget the Words
56.quote: 言者所以在意，得意而忘言。
56.quoteEn: Words are there for the meaning. Get the meaning and forget the words.
56.body: The Laozi says 知者不言，言者不知: one who knows does not speak; one who speaks does not know. Taken hard, the line condemns itself, since it is spoken. Zhuangzi offers a softer reading. A fish trap is for fish; when you have the fish you forget the trap. A snare is for rabbits. Words are for meaning. He does not say words are useless. He says they are tools to put down. Then comes his wistful joke: 'Where can I find someone who has forgotten words, so that I can have a word with him?' This app is all words about a text that distrusts words. What have you caught so far, and can you put the trap down?

56.source: Cao Xueqin, Story of the Stone, ch. 22 (Baoyu's Chan verse, and Daiyu's addition)
56.title: No Place to Stand
56.quoteEn: When nothing can be called proof, that is the ground to stand on.
56.body: After a family quarrel, Baoyu decides he has seen through everything and writes a Chan-style verse. This is its last line. He is proud of it. Daiyu reads it and says: good, but not finished. First she tests him with a riddle on his own name, and he cannot answer. Then she adds two lines of her own: 無立足境，是方乾淨. 'No ground to stand on at all: only that is clean.' The girls laugh and tell him to stop playing at Chan. The Laozi's 知者不言 is at work in the scene. Baoyu has announced his insight, so he does not have it. Daiyu removes the last foothold, and she does it in words too, as a game. Is there any way to say this that does not stand somewhere?

57.source: Sunzi, Art of War, ch. 5 (Shi, Force)
57.title: The Straight and the Surprise
57.quoteEn: In all fighting, meet them with the straight, and win with the surprise.
57.body: The Laozi opens with three lines that divide the world: 以正治國，以奇用兵，以無事取天下. Rule a state with the straight; use weapons with the surprise; take the world by having no business. The pair 正 and 奇 belongs to the soldiers, and here is Sunzi using it. For him the two feed each other without end, like a ring. The Laozi grants the soldiers their rule and then sets a third thing above both. Later in the passage it shows why. The more laws and orders are displayed, the more thieves there are. The sage says: 我無為而民自化, 'I do not force, and the people change by themselves'. Where are you using surprise when you could use nothing?

58.source: Cao Xueqin, Story of the Stone, ch. 1 (Zhen Shiyin's gloss on the Daoist's song)
58.title: Yesterday's Coat, Today's Robe
58.quote: 因嫌紗帽小，致使鎖枷扛；昨憐破襖寒，今嫌紫蟒長。
58.quoteEn: Because he thought his gauze cap too small, he came to carry the prisoner's collar. Yesterday he pitied his torn coat for its cold; today he finds the purple court robe too long.
58.body: Zhen Shiyin answers the Daoist's song with a longer one of his own. It runs through rooms once full of officials' tablets and now hung with cobwebs, and through chests of gold that end in beggary. Then he takes the Daoist's bag and walks away with him. The Laozi says 禍兮福之所倚，福兮禍之所伏: disaster is what fortune leans on; fortune is where disaster hides. 孰知其極? Who knows the turning point? The song gives the answer of experience. No one knows, and each man thinks the wheel has stopped at him. The official wants a bigger cap and so earns the collar. Where are you treating a point on the wheel as a place to stand?

58.source: Sunzi, Art of War, ch. 8 (Jiu bian, The Nine Changes)
58.title: Gain and Harm Mixed
58.quote: 是故智者之慮，必雜於利害
58.quoteEn: So the thinking of the wise always mixes gain and harm.
58.body: The Laozi sees fortune and disaster curled inside each other and asks who can know where one ends. Sunzi makes this a habit of mind for a commander. In a bad position, think of the gain in it, and the task can be carried through. In a good position, think of the harm in it, and the trouble can be undone. This is 禍兮福之所倚 as a working method. The Laozi takes one more step and turns it on the ruler's manner. So the sage is 方而不割: square and does not cut; bright and does not dazzle. If each thing holds its opposite, hard edges are a mistake. In today's good news, what is the harm? In today's bad news, what is the gain?

61.title: What Is Full Flows to the Low
61.quote: 天道虧盈而益謙，地道變盈而流謙
61.quoteEn: Heaven's way lessens what is full and adds to what is modest. Earth's way changes what is full and flows toward what is modest.
61.body: The Laozi says 大國者下流: a great state is the low reach of a river, where all the world's streams meet. It is the female of the world, who wins by stillness and by lying low. Hexagram 15 is a mountain hidden under the earth, and its comment says the same of heaven, earth, spirits, and people: all four move against the full and toward the low. The Yijing speaks here of a person's character. The Laozi applies it to states, and to the strong first of all. 大者宜為下: it is the great one that ought to take the low place. A small state that bows is only being prudent. Where are you the larger party? Do you go low there?

63.source: Sunzi, Art of War, ch. 4 (Xing, Form)
63.title: No Name for Wisdom, No Credit for Courage
63.quote: 故善戰者之勝也，無智名，無勇功。
63.quoteEn: So the victories of one good at war bring no name for wisdom and no credit for courage.
63.body: The Laozi says 圖難於其易，為大於其細: plan for the hard while it is easy; do the great while it is small. Sunzi draws the result that few people like. The best general wins where winning is easy, over an enemy who has already lost. So no one praises him. To lift an autumn hair is not called strength. The crowd cheers the desperate rescue, which is a sign that someone acted late. The Laozi adds: the sage never does great things, and so can complete the great. Both texts ask you to give up being seen as a hero. Which problem could you solve this week while it is still too small to earn thanks?

64.source: Musashi, Book of Five Rings, Water scroll (水之巻), closing words
64.title: One Step at a Time
64.quote: 千里の道もひと足宛はこぶ也。
64.quoteEn: Even a road of a thousand ri is walked one step at a time.
64.body: This is the Laozi's 千里之行，始於足下, a journey of a thousand li begins under the foot, in Japanese dress. By Musashi's day the saying had been a proverb across East Asia for many centuries, and he uses it as common wisdom without naming a source. In the preface he says he borrows no old words from Buddhism or Confucianism. The proverb slipped in all the same. He applies it to practice: study each item, test it against opponents, do not hurry. The Laozi's line sits in a different argument. It is about acting on things while they are small and not yet formed. Musashi hears patience. The Laozi means timing. What is under your foot now?

64.source: Yijing, hexagram 2 Kun (The Receptive), first line
64.title: Frost Underfoot
64.quoteEn: Treading on frost. Hard ice is coming.
64.body: The Laozi says 其未兆易謀: what shows no sign yet is easy to plan for. What is brittle is easy to break, what is tiny is easy to scatter. Act on it before it exists. The first line of Kun trains the same sense. The foot feels a thin crust of frost. Nothing is wrong yet. The line simply reads the season forward. A tree an arm-span wide grows from a fine tip, says the Laozi, and a nine-story tower rises from a basket of earth. The frost line is the dark twin of those pictures. Small beginnings build towers, and they also build ice. What frost did you step on this week and not mention to anyone?

66.title: All Rivers Go Home to It
66.quote: 天下之水，莫大於海，萬川歸之
66.quoteEn: Of all the waters under heaven, none is greater than the sea. The ten thousand rivers go home to it.
66.body: The Laozi asks why rivers and seas can be kings of the hundred valleys, and answers: 以其善下之, because they are good at being below them. Zhuangzi's sea god, Ruo of the North Sea, says the same of himself, and then refuses the crown. The rivers pour in without end and the sea is not full. Yet set between heaven and earth, he says, the four seas are like a small hollow in a great marsh. So the Laozi uses the sea to teach rulers how to lead: stay low and people will not feel your weight. Zhuangzi uses the sea to teach that even the lowest and largest is small. Which lesson does a leader need first?

67.source: Cao Xueqin, Story of the Stone, ch. 3 (second of the mock verses on Baoyu)
67.title: First in Uselessness
67.quote: 天下無能第一，古今不肖無雙。
67.quoteEn: In all the world, first in having no ability. From old times to now, without equal in being good for nothing.
67.body: The Laozi's speaker reports what people say: 天下皆謂我道大，似不肖. All the world says my Dao is great, and seems like nothing proper. The term 不肖 means 'not resembling', unlike one's worthy father, and so a failure. The speaker accepts it: because it is great, it resembles nothing. If it resembled something, it would long ago have become small. The verse on Baoyu uses the same word. He is 不肖 without rival: he will not study for office, and he prefers the company of girls to that of men of rank. The novel wears the insult as the Laozi does. Then the Laozi names three treasures: compassion, thrift, and not daring to be first in the world. Baoyu has the first. Does he have the other two?

67.source: Sunzi, Art of War, ch. 10 (Di xing, Terrain)
67.title: Soldiers as One's Own Children
67.quote: 視卒如嬰兒，故可以與之赴深溪
67.quoteEn: Look on the troops as infants, and so you can go with them into the deep ravine.
67.body: The Laozi's first treasure is 慈, the tender care of a parent, and it makes a claim about war: 慈故能勇, with compassion one can be brave. In attack it wins; in defense it holds. Sunzi agrees from the general's side. Treat soldiers as beloved sons and they will die with you. Then he adds a warning. If you are kind and cannot give orders, they are spoiled children and no use. For Sunzi, care is a bond that makes an army work. For the Laozi, care is the root, and courage without it is called death. The Laozi even says heaven guards with compassion those it would save. Is your kindness to those you lead a method or a root?

68.source: Sunzi, Art of War, ch. 12 (Huo gong, Attack by Fire)
68.title: No Army Raised in Anger
68.quote: 主不可以怒而興師，將不可以慍而致戰。
68.quoteEn: A ruler must not raise an army out of anger. A general must not give battle out of resentment.
68.body: The Laozi says 善戰者不怒: one good at fighting is not angry. Sunzi gives the same rule to the two people who can start a war, and gives his reason. Anger passes. What anger destroys does not come back. Move when it serves, he says, and stop when it does not. The Laozi sets the line in a list of four: the good officer is not warlike, the good fighter is not angry, the good winner does not engage, the good employer of people goes below them. It calls this 不爭之德, the power of not contending. Sunzi's calm is good judgment. The Laozi's calm is a kind of strength in itself. What decision are you about to make while angry?

68.title: The Wooden Rooster
68.quote: 望之似木雞矣，其德全矣。
68.quoteEn: Look at it from a distance and it is like a rooster of wood. Its de is complete.
68.body: A trainer raises a fighting cock for a king. After ten days the king asks if it is ready. Not yet; it struts and trusts its own force. Ten more days. Not yet; it still starts at sounds and shadows. Ten more. Not yet; it glares and is full of spirit. At last the trainer says this. Other cocks crow and it does not change. None dares to face it; they turn and run. The Laozi says 善勝敵者不與: one good at defeating the enemy does not join with him. Zhuangzi shows the stages of getting there, and each stage to be dropped looks like strength: swagger, alertness, fierce spirit. Which stage are you in?

68.source: Musashi, Book of Five Rings, Fire scroll (火之巻), on 'letting go of the hilt'
68.title: Letting Go of the Hilt
68.quote: 無刀にて勝心有、又、太刀にてかたざる心あり。
68.quoteEn: There is a spirit of winning with no sword. There is also a spirit of not winning with the sword.
68.body: This is one of the shortest items in the Fire scroll, and Musashi will not explain it: the heart goes many ways here, he says, and it cannot be written down. Train well. So a man who built his life on the two-sword school leaves a note that the sword is not the point. The Laozi's 善為士者不武 says a good officer is not warlike, and its 不爭之德 names a power that needs no contest. Musashi's line is not pacifism. It comes from a fighter who had seen that the win is decided before the hands move, and that a hand locked on its weapon is not free. What is the hilt you cannot let go of?

69.source: Sunzi, Art of War, ch. 4 (Xing, Form)
69.title: First, Be Unbeatable
69.quote: 先為不可勝，以待敵之可勝。
69.quoteEn: First make yourself impossible to defeat, and so wait for the enemy to become possible to defeat.
69.body: The Laozi quotes soldiers here: 用兵有言, 'those who use weapons have a saying'. The saying is 吾不敢為主而為客: I do not dare to be the host; I would be the guest. I do not dare advance an inch; I fall back a foot. Sunzi's chapter on form may be close to the tradition the Laozi heard. The masters of old secured themselves first and waited. Being unbeatable depends on me, he says; the enemy being beatable depends on him. Victory can be known and cannot be made. The Laozi then moves into its own tongue: 行無行, to march with no march, to roll up a sleeve with no arm. Sunzi waits for an opening. Is the Laozi waiting for anything?

69.source: Musashi, Book of Five Rings, Fire scroll (火之巻), on the three initiatives
69.title: The Initiative Comes First
69.quote: 先と云事、兵法の第一也。
69.quoteEn: The thing called the initiative is the first matter of strategy.
69.body: Here is a master who says the opposite of this passage. The Laozi's soldier does not dare to be host and would be guest. He gives up a foot before he takes an inch.
