Musashi says that in every fight there are three ways to take the lead, and nothing else: when you attack, when the enemy attacks, and when both attack. Even in waiting you must hold the lead. He hates to be led around: 'press down the pillow' and do not let the other raise his head. Is this a plain contradiction? Perhaps. But look at Musashi's second kind: to appear weak as the enemy comes, and take him as he slackens. And the Laozi's guest is not passive. 禍莫大於輕敵, it says: no disaster is greater than taking the enemy lightly.

70.source: Cao Xueqin, Story of the Stone, ch. 1 (the monk and the Daoist enter the human world)
70.title: Rags Outside, Jade Inside
70.quote: 那僧則癩頭跣腳，那道則跛足蓬頭，瘋瘋癲癲
70.quoteEn: The monk had a scabby head and bare feet. The Daoist was lame, with wild hair. Both were raving like madmen.
70.body: On the mountain of the gods, these two were noble in bone and bright in spirit. When they walk into a city street they look like this. For the rest of the novel they turn up at each crisis, and nearly everyone takes them for lunatics. The Laozi says 聖人被褐懷玉: the sage wears coarse cloth and carries jade in the breast. In the novel the picture is nearly literal, for these two are the keepers of the jade. The Laozi's speaker is sad: 吾言甚易知, my words are very easy to know, and no one under heaven can know them. Those who understand are few. Who came to your door in rough cloth, and what did you do?

70.title: Easy to Know, Simple to Follow
70.quoteEn: What is easy is easy to know. What is simple is easy to follow.
70.body: The Laozi says 吾言甚易知，甚易行: my words are very easy to know and very easy to practice. Then it adds, with some pain, that no one in the world can know or practice them. The Great Treatise makes the hopeful half of this claim about the Yijing's two first powers. Heaven takes charge through the easy; earth completes through the simple. And so people draw near and the work succeeds. The Treatise expects that the easy will win followers. The Laozi has learned that the easy is exactly what people walk past, since they want something worthy of their effort. Both may be right at different times. What very easy thing have you been told many times?

71.source: Musashi, Book of Five Rings, Void scroll (空之巻)
71.title: Not Every Blank Is the Void
71.quote: 物をわきまへざる所を空と見る所、実の空にはあらず。
71.quoteEn: To take the state of not understanding things for the void: that is not the true void.
71.body: The Laozi packs a warning into eight characters: 知不知上，不知知病. To know that you do not know is best. Not to know and to think you know is a sickness. Musashi guards the other side of the same door. There is a not-knowing that is only ignorance, he says, and people call it emptiness. A warrior who has not learned his craft and is lost in doubt is not in the void. The true void comes after the craft, when nothing is left dark. So the two texts fence the word from both sides. Not all knowing is knowledge, and not all blankness is wisdom. When you say 'I don't know', which kind is it?

76.source: Musashi, Book of Five Rings, Water scroll (水之巻), on gripping the sword
76.title: The Fixed Hand Is a Dead Hand
76.quote: いつくは、しぬる手也。いつかざるハ、いきる手なり。
76.quoteEn: To be fixed in place is the dead hand. Not to be fixed is the living hand.
76.body: The Laozi says 人之生也柔弱，其死也堅強: a person at birth is soft and weak; at death, stiff and hard. Grass and trees are tender alive and dry when dead. So the stiff are 'followers of death' and the soft are 'followers of life'. Musashi finds the same law in the grip. Hold the sword with the thumb and forefinger loose and the lower fingers firm. He hates a hand or blade that has settled, and uses the Laozi's own two categories, the dead and the living. He knew it from the cost of error. The Laozi even adds a military note: 兵強則不勝, a stiff army does not win. Check your hands and jaw now. Are they living?

77.title: Decrease in Its Season
77.quoteEn: Decreasing and increasing, filling and emptying: these go along with the time.
77.body: The Laozi compares heaven's way to drawing a bow. The high end comes down and the low end comes up. 天之道，損有餘而補不足: heaven's way takes from what has too much and adds to what has too little. The human way, it says bitterly, does the reverse. The Yijing has a whole hexagram named with the same verb, 損, to decrease. Its comment is cooler. Decrease and increase each have a season. The moral heat is the Laozi's own. It sees a world where the short are taxed to feed the long. Then it asks: who can have a surplus and offer it to the world? Only one who has the Dao. What do you hold that is 有餘?

78.source: Sunzi, Art of War, ch. 5 (Shi, Force)
78.title: Water That Moves Stones
78.quote: 激水之疾，至於漂石者，勢也
78.quoteEn: The rush of surging water reaches the point where it floats stones along. This is force of position.
78.body: The Laozi says nothing in the world is softer and weaker than water, and yet for attacking the hard and strong nothing can beat it: 天下莫柔弱於水，而攻堅強者莫之能勝. It gives no cause. Sunzi supplies one, and he is exact. Water moves stones through 勢, the force that builds when a thing is gathered and let go from a height. It is like a drawn crossbow. So water's softness is only half the story. Its strength is in the arrangement. But the Laozi then takes the image somewhere Sunzi never goes. The one who accepts the state's dirt and its bad luck is the true lord. Water wins by accepting. What does your softness accept?

78.title: The Swimmer at Lüliang
78.quoteEn: I follow the way of the water and do not set up anything private against it.
78.body: Confucius watches a waterfall so fierce that no fish or turtle can swim below it. He sees a man in the foam and sends his students to save him. The man comes out singing. Does he have a method? No, he says. I go in with the swirl and come out with the upwelling. The Laozi praises water from the bank: 弱之勝強，柔之勝剛, the weak overcomes the strong and the soft overcomes the hard. All the world knows this, it adds, and no one can practice it. Zhuangzi shows a man who can. His secret is the missing 私, the private will set against the flow. Where are you swimming against a current you could ride?

80.source: Zhuangzi, ch. 12 (Tian di, Heaven and Earth)
80.title: The Gardener Refuses the Machine
80.quote: 有機械者必有機事，有機事者必有機心。
80.quoteEn: Where there are machines there will be machine business. Where there is machine business there will be a machine heart.
80.body: An old gardener carries water from a well in a jar, one trip at a time. A student of Confucius tells him of the well-sweep, a lever that waters a hundred plots in a day with little effort. The gardener laughs, a little angrily. I know of it, he says. I would be ashamed to use it. The Laozi's small state has 什伯之器而不用: tools that do the work of ten or a hundred men, and they are not used. It has boats and carts, and no one rides them. The gardener gives the reason the Laozi leaves out. The harm is not in the tool. It is in the scheming heart that the tool trains. Which of your tools has given you its heart?

80.title: The Passage, Quoted
80.quote: 雞狗之音相聞，民至老死而不相往來。
80.quoteEn: The sounds of roosters and dogs reach from one to the other, and the people grow old and die without going back and forth.
80.body: This chapter of the Zhuangzi repeats the end of this passage nearly word for word: knotted cords for records, food found sweet, clothes found beautiful, the neighbor state within sight. It is one of our oldest witnesses to the Laozi's text. And it changes the tense. The Laozi's lines can be read as a wish or a thought-experiment. The Zhuangzi chapter places the picture in the past, under a list of twelve ancient rulers, and says 'that was perfect order'. Then it turns on its own age, where people stretch their necks and run after any famous teacher. So a quiet image has become a lost golden age and a weapon. Do you read the small state as a memory, a plan, or a mirror?

80.source: Cao Xueqin, Story of the Stone, ch. 17 (Baoyu on the model farm in the garden)
80.title: The Village Built for Show
80.quote: 分明見得人力穿鑿扭捏而成
80.quoteEn: It is plain to see that it was bored out and twisted into shape by human effort.
80.body: A noble family builds a pleasure garden for an imperial visit. One corner is a toy farm with mud walls, a well-sweep, and rows of vegetables. The master of the house says it stirs in him a wish to go back to the land. His son Baoyu says this, and is nearly thrown out. The scene is a hard comment on how the Laozi's 小國寡民, the small state with few people, was used by later ages. The rich loved the picture and built copies of it inside their walls. The Laozi's villagers 'find their food sweet' and stay home. They do not visit a set. When simplicity is something you buy, what have you bought?

81.source: Cao Xueqin, Story of the Stone, ch. 1 (the author's quatrain)
81.title: Pages of Wild Words
81.quote: 滿紙荒唐言，一把辛酸淚！都云作者痴，誰解其中味？
81.quoteEn: Pages full of wild talk, a handful of bitter tears. All say the author is a fool. Who can tell the taste inside?
81.body: The Laozi's last passage begins 信言不美，美言不信: true words are not beautiful; beautiful words are not true. Cao Xueqin's verse about his own book accepts a harder name than 'not beautiful'. He calls his pages 荒唐, wild and absurd. His characters carry names that pun on 'true things hidden' and 'false words in village speech'. A novel is 'false' on every page, and he claims it holds a truth that plain report could not. So here is a test case for the Laozi's rule. Is a fiction a beautiful word, and so not to be trusted? Or is its open falseness a kind of honesty? The Laozi itself is fine writing that warns against fine writing. Who can tell the taste inside?
